prompt: `agent.py` answered Bia's question through `recorder.py`, and the log showed two requests. How many input tokens did the second request carry?
In the course's lab, `agent.py`'s loop is written `for step in range(1, ___):`, so no reply from the model can make a run take more than five steps.
On the autonomy dial, the course's `agent.py` hands some decisions to the model and keeps others. Which decision stays with the programmer?

choices.text: How many steps a run is allowed
choices.why: Right. `range(1, 6)` is the programmer's, and no reply from the model changes it.

choices.text: Which of the two tools to call next
choices.why: No. That choice is handed to the model, and it is what makes `agent.py` an agent.

choices.text: Whether to answer now or keep looking things up
choices.why: No. `agent.py` gives the model the choice of when to answer, inside the host's limit.

choices.text: What order id goes into a `get_order` call
choices.why: No. `get_order` got `M-1042` because the model put it there.

prompt: Where does the course's `agent.py` keep what it knows about a run between one step and the next?

choices.text: In the model, which remembers the earlier requests of the same run
choices.why: No. A model API keeps nothing between requests.

choices.text: In the list `messages`, which is sent in full on every request
choices.why: Right. The conversation is the agent's whole state; each step sends everything again.

choices.text: In `shop.py`, which records each call it has run so far
choices.why: No. `shop.py` holds plain functions; nothing is remembered outside the conversation.

choices.text: In the recorder's `requests.jsonl`, which the loop reads back at every step
choices.why: No. That log is for people inspecting runs; `agent.py` never reads it.

prompt: With `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` pointed at port 11435, `agent.py` ends with `anthropic.APIConnectionError: Connection error.` What does that tell you?

choices.text: `ollama.env` never reached this shell, so the library found no key
choices.why: No. A missing key reads `Could not resolve authentication method`; here a key was found and nothing answered.

choices.text: Nothing answered at that address: the recorder was not running
choices.why: Right. The same line appears when Ollama itself is stopped, and `ollama --version` then warns too.

choices.text: The Python in use is older than 3.12, which `shop.py` needs
choices.why: No. That fails with `module 'math' has no attribute 'sumprod'`.

choices.text: The model's name was mistyped, so Ollama has no model by it
choices.why: No. Ollama answers that with `pull model manifest: file does not exist`.

prompt: After the context setting was written, `ollama ps` still shows 4096 in its CONTEXT column. What does the course say is wrong?

choices.text: The model was pulled before the setting existed and must be pulled again
choices.why: No. The setting is Ollama's, not the model's; pulling again changes nothing.

choices.text: The service needs a restart, with the setting in its own environment
choices.why: Right. On Linux it belongs in the service's environment, not your shell's, and Ollama reads it only when it starts.

choices.text: 4096 is the most `llama3.2:3b` accepts, so the setting is capped
choices.why: No. The course runs the model at 8192, and `ollama ps` shows that once the setting takes.

choices.text: The setting only applies to a conversation once it passes 4096 tokens
choices.why: No. The column shows the context Ollama gave the model; 4096 means the setting did not take.

prompt: In the course's errors-compound table, each step of a run is right with probability 0.99, independently. To two decimal places, what is the chance that a 20-step run is right throughout?
Marginalia sorts the actions an agent might take by how far back they can be taken. Put the kinds in order, from the one an agent can be given most freely to the one nothing undoes.
items: reads, such as `get_order`
drafts a person may not send
reversible writes, such as a hold on an order
writes with a cost to reverse, such as a refund
irreversible or external actions, such as an email

prompt: Which of these are among the five workflow patterns that Anthropic's *Building effective agents* names? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Chaining
choices.why: Right. The output of one call is the input of the next.

choices.text: Routing
choices.why: Right. One call classifies the input, and code sends it down a fixed branch.

choices.text: A loop in which the model picks every next tool
choices.why: No. That is an agent; none of the five lets the model decide, step by step, what to do next.

choices.text: Orchestrator and workers
choices.why: Right. One call splits the task and a worker call handles each part.

choices.text: Plan, act and revise
choices.why: No. That is the approach lesson 5 builds for an agent, not one of the article's five.

prompt: Marginalia's router answered Bia's return question with only `M-1042 is delivered, delivered on 2026-09-24`. If the team wants the router to answer such messages, what does the course say it costs?

choices.text: Replacing the router with the agent for every message
choices.why: No. One known kind of message needs a branch, not an agent's requests and tokens on every message.

choices.text: A second model call per message to read the window
choices.why: No. The branch the lesson describes computes the window in code, with no further model call.

choices.text: One more branch: an afternoon, and no extra requests
choices.why: Right. Look up the order, compute the window, print it; the label request stays the only one.

choices.text: A larger `max_tokens`, so that the label says more
choices.why: No. The label is one word by design; what is missing is a branch.

prompt: Of the five proposals at Marginalia, 'Write the nightly stock report' was made plain automation. Why?

choices.text: Its path depends on what each lookup returns
choices.why: No. That is an agent's shape; this report is a query, a table and an email.

choices.text: There is no free text in it to read, so a model would only add a way for the numbers to go wrong
choices.why: Right. A query, a table and an email to two people need no model.

choices.text: It runs too many times a day to pay for an agent
choices.why: No. It runs once a night; volume was not the reason.

choices.text: Its result is something only a person is able to check
choices.why: No. The lesson gives no such reason, and a stock count is checkable.

prompt: The course says 'reversible' is not a property of an action in the abstract. Which example does it give?

choices.text: Sending an email is reversible until the customer opens it
choices.why: No. The lesson's table puts sending an email among the actions nothing undoes.

choices.text: Reading an order is reversible only when the read is logged
choices.why: No. A read needs no undo; reading again is free.

choices.text: A note on an order is reversible only for the agent that wrote it
choices.why: No. A note is a reversible write, undone by removing it.

choices.text: Deleting a file is reversible only where a trash folder is kept
choices.why: Right. Undo is a feature built into tools: soft deletes, holds, drafts.

prompt: In the ReAct paper (Yao and colleagues, 2022), what could the model do on the question-answering and fact-checking tasks, HotpotQA and FEVER?

choices.text: Call tools declared as JSON Schema in each request
choices.why: No. The paper's model knew nothing about tools; a regular expression found actions in plain text.

choices.text: Search, look up and finish, over Wikipedia
choices.why: Right. On ALFWorld and WebShop the actions were moves in the environment instead.

choices.text: Move through a simulated online shop to find products
choices.why: No. That was WebShop, one of the interactive tasks.

choices.text: Reason in chain of thought with no tool of any kind
choices.why: No. That was what it was compared against, and it made up facts it could have looked up.

prompt: Why does the size of a tool's result cost more the longer an agent's run lasts?

choices.text: It is resent in every later request
choices.why: Right. In a twenty-step run, an observation returned at step 1 is sent nineteen more times.

choices.text: The price of each token rises as a conversation grows
choices.why: No. The lesson's point is how many times the result is sent, not a changing price.

choices.text: Older results are dropped once the context window is full
choices.why: No. These loops keep every result; an observation that does not fit ends the run.

choices.text: The model rereads only the latest result at each new step
choices.why: No. Each request carries the whole conversation, every earlier result included.

prompt: The course trims order M-1047's observation to `status`, `delivered_on` and `total`, then warns that leaving out `customer_id` has a cost. What is it?

choices.text: The provider refuses a tool result with no customer field in it
choices.why: No. Nothing in the API asks for that field.

choices.text: Without it, the 28-token object would no longer parse as JSON
choices.why: No. The trimmed object is valid JSON either way.

choices.text: Lesson 17 needs it to check that the person asking owns the order
choices.why: Right. A field left out is one the model cannot use; the compromise is a tool per purpose.

choices.text: The refund amount is worked out from the customer's own record in the shop
choices.why: No. A refund's amount comes from the order's `total`, 7780 cents, which the trimmed object keeps.

prompt: The course's `react_native.py` writes each step to `trace.jsonl`, keeping only the first 80 characters of each result. Why that cut?

choices.text: The trace file has a fixed line length of 80
choices.why: No. JSON lines have no such limit; the cut is a choice.

choices.text: The model reads only the first 80 characters of a result
choices.why: No. The whole result goes to the model; only the trace is cut.

choices.text: Enough to recognise a result without copying a customer's whole order into a log
choices.why: Right. A trace is data about people: log what explains a run and no more.

choices.text: Longer results are refused by the host before they run
choices.why: No. The host passes the whole output back as the `tool_result`.

prompt: An agent runs on a model that reasons at length before answering and returns that reasoning summarised, encrypted or not at all. What does the course say this does to the agent's trace?

choices.text: The thoughts become the record, since they are fuller
choices.why: No. When thoughts and calls disagree, the calls are the record.

choices.text: Fewer thoughts to read; the calls become the whole trace
choices.why: Right. Some APIs also require that reasoning to be passed back unchanged in the next request.

choices.text: The trace is no longer needed, since the reasoning is checked
choices.why: No. Nothing checks hidden reasoning, and the calls still have to be logged.

choices.text: The host must decrypt the reasoning before it logs the run
choices.why: No. The lesson says some APIs want it passed back unchanged, not decrypted.

prompt: A text-ReAct program already stops generation at `Observation:`. Which jobs does the course say are still the parser's? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Run only the first `Action:` line and discard the rest
choices.why: Right. A second action was chosen without seeing the first one's result.

choices.text: Run every `Action:` line, in the order the model wrote them
choices.why: No. Only the first was chosen with what was known; the rest are discarded.

choices.text: Distrust an `Answer:` that follows an `Action:` in the same reply
choices.why: Right. It was written before the action ran, so it does not rest on the result.

choices.text: Look for `Answer:` before looking for an action
choices.why: No. That order is why step 3 of the first run ended before its search ran; looking for an action first is safer.

choices.text: Return a short error as the observation when an action does not parse
choices.why: Right. The model then gets to try again instead of the program raising.

prompt: In the course's `wires.py`, one question went to `llama3.2:3b` over three wire formats, and each reply carried the same tool call. Match each API to the field that said why the reply stopped.

pairs.right: `done_reason: "stop"`, with the call in the message

right_distractors: `finishReason: "STOP"`, with the call in the parts

prompt: In the course's `tools.py`, every tool's schema sets `___: false`, so a call carrying an argument nobody declared, such as `verbose`, is refused.
The course's `tools.py` gives order ids the pattern `^M-[0-9]{4}$`. Why does the lesson advise against a pattern on a free-text search query?

choices.text: It would refuse real questions
choices.why: Right. Be strict where a mistake costs something: an id has one shape, a question does not.

choices.text: Providers do not accept `pattern` on string arguments
choices.why: No. `tools.py` uses `pattern` on order ids, and the validator enforces it.

choices.text: The model reads a pattern as an order to stop searching
choices.why: No. The lesson describes no such effect; the cost is refusing legitimate questions.

choices.text: Checking a pattern makes each search noticeably slower
choices.why: No. Speed is not the lesson's reason; refusing real questions is.

prompt: Which of these does the course say must stay out of a tool's description?

choices.text: The unit of the amounts the tool returns
choices.why: No. Units belong in it: `find_books` says prices in cents.

choices.text: What the tool changes in the world, if anything
choices.why: No. A side effect the description leaves out is a trap for the model and the reviewer.

choices.text: An internal URL or a key
choices.why: Right. Descriptions go to the provider with every request and appear in traces, so a secret there is published.

choices.text: When to use it rather than a close tool
choices.why: No. That is part of a good description when another tool is near it.

prompt: A model's reply asks for two tools, and the host cannot run one of them. What does the course say the host sends back for that one?

choices.text: Nothing; the model will notice the missing result on its own and ask for the tool again
choices.why: No. Anthropic's API refuses a conversation in which a call has no result, with a `400` naming the call.

choices.text: The other call's result alone, so that the model is not confused
choices.why: No. That is the `--drop-one` bug: Anthropic's API refuses it, and where nothing refuses, the model must guess.

choices.text: A result with that call's id, marked as an error, saying why it did not run
choices.why: Right. Every `tool_use` needs a `tool_result` with its id in the very next message.

choices.text: A new request with the failed call removed from the reply
choices.why: No. That drops the call silently, which the lesson says never to do.

prompt: In the course's lab, `issue_refund` refunded all 3480 cents of M-1042. A later call with a new key, `ticket-5521-again`, was refused with `0 left to refund`. Which defence refused it?

choices.text: The idempotency key, which had been used before
choices.why: No. `ticket-5521-again` was new, so the call was treated as a new refund.

choices.text: The balance check in `shop.refund`
choices.why: Right. The key stops a retry of one intent; the balance check stops a second intent that would overdraw.

choices.text: The schema, because `cents` was larger than the order's total
choices.why: No. The schema asks only for at least 1 cent; it checks form, never facts.

choices.text: The model, which saw the first refund earlier in the conversation
choices.why: No. These calls were made directly through `run_tool`, with no model involved.

prompt: In the course, `agent.py --max-seconds 2` stopped with `time budget: 2.0 s`, but its first request alone had taken 119835 ms. By the lesson's count, how many seconds late did the check come?
Why does the course's `agent.py` count three budgets (steps, tokens and seconds) rather than one?

choices.text: The provider bills steps, tokens and seconds as separate items
choices.why: No. Money is tokens times their price; the three budgets protect against different failures.

choices.text: Three limits give the model more room to plan its work
choices.why: No. None of the limits is mentioned to the model.

choices.text: They fail differently: many tiny steps, one huge document, slow tools
choices.why: Right. One limit alone would leave the other two failure modes open.

choices.text: A step limit is checked only after a request
choices.why: No. All three are checked before every request.

prompt: The course ran the gift-and-order question on `llama3.2:3b` with `--max-seconds 2`. How far had the run got when it stopped?

choices.text: It had sent no request: the clock had run out before the first one
choices.why: No. The budget is checked before each request, and the first went out at once; the recorder logged it.

choices.text: It had written a plan and stopped before acting on it
choices.why: No. No plan was written: `done` and `not_done` are empty, and the handoff says so.

choices.text: One reply had run, with two tool calls in it and no plan
choices.why: Right. The check before the second request stopped the run, 118 seconds late.

choices.text: It had answered through `finish`, and the time check threw the answer away
choices.why: No. That reply called no `finish`; the run that did was the token run, which ended `answered`.

prompt: A design gives the model a `continue_working(extra_steps: 10)` tool. What is wrong with it, according to the course?

choices.text: A JSON Schema cannot express a number of extra steps
choices.why: No. An integer argument is easy to declare; the problem is who holds the limit.

choices.text: The model grants itself more room exactly when a looping model thinks it useful
choices.why: Right. A limit the model changes is no limit; the counter belongs to the host.

choices.text: Each call to it costs one more request to the model
choices.why: No. Cost is not the point; the model would be setting its own budget.

choices.text: The model is not told how many steps it has used
choices.why: No. Informing the model is harmless; handing it the limit is the flaw.

prompt: An agent keeps rewriting its plan, and no new tool result arrives between the rewrites. What does the course suggest the host do?

choices.text: Mark the remaining steps `done` so that the run reaches `finish` with an answer
choices.why: No. Marking an undone step done is false; `dropped` exists for a step abandoned on purpose.

choices.text: Raise the step limit so the plan has time to settle
choices.why: No. A run that makes no progress is what a limit is there to stop.

choices.text: Count plan updates with no new result after them, and stop after a few
choices.why: Right. It is the 'no progress' row of lesson 3's table, applied to plans.

choices.text: Send the plan back with a request to keep it brief
choices.why: No. The remedy the lesson gives is a counter in the host, not a prompt.

prompt: Put the course's handoff run for order M-1046 (`multi.py --handoff`) in order.
items: The triage agent makes one request and calls `transfer_to_orders`
The host starts the orders specialist on the customer's message
The specialist searches the help centre, without looking the order up
The specialist answers the customer itself

prompt: In the course's `multi.py`, the catalogue specialist is given only `find_books`. What does that buy if something persuades it to look up an order?

choices.text: The orchestrator notices and asks the orders specialist instead
choices.why: No. Nothing in `multi.py` watches for that; the protection is the missing tool.

choices.text: Its system prompt forbids it, and the model obeys
choices.why: No. A prompt is a request; the protection is that no tool exists for it.

choices.text: There is no tool for it to call
choices.why: Right. Least privilege per agent: an agent that reads untrusted content should be one that cannot act.

choices.text: The host logs the attempt and raises an alarm for a person
choices.why: No. `multi.py` has no such alarm.

prompt: A team argues that its multi-agent design is better because each specialist is an expert at its job. What does the course answer?

choices.text: Specialists gain expertise from longer system prompts
choices.why: No. The lesson's reasons are context, tools, privilege and parallel work, not expertise.

choices.text: Expertise appears only when the orchestrator runs on a larger model
choices.why: No. Every agent here uses the same model, and the lesson ties no benefit to model size.

choices.text: The same model is behind every agent, so none knows more
choices.why: Right. Every agent in `multi.py` is `llama3.2:3b`; a split changes what each agent sees and is allowed to do.

choices.text: Expertise is real, but it shows only in the handoff shape
choices.why: No. Neither shape makes a specialist more expert.

prompt: The course answered one question about order M-1043 and a science-fiction book twice: with an orchestrator and two specialists, and with a single agent. Where did the orchestrated run's extra tokens come from?

choices.text: The specialists looked up more data than the single agent
choices.why: No. Each specialist made one tool call, the same lookups the single agent made.

choices.text: Each agent's own prompt and tool definitions, resent per request, and the orchestrator reading the answers
choices.why: Right. None of that work answered the customer; it is the price of the boundary.

choices.text: The orchestrator's final answer was a longer text
choices.why: No. Its answer was the shorter one: it left the book out.

choices.text: Retries after the catalogue specialist's call failed
choices.why: No. No call failed in that run.

prompt: In a longer conversation, a handoff has to decide what the receiving agent is given. What does the course say about that choice?

choices.text: Pass every turn, so that the specialist sees all of it
choices.why: No. Passing everything carries other agents' data and cost into an agent that may not need it.

choices.text: Let the triage agent summarise the history in its tool's arguments
choices.why: No. `transfer_to_orders` takes no arguments; what moves is the conversation.

choices.text: Pass nothing, since a specialist starts from a blank conversation
choices.why: No. The specialist needs at least the customer's message to answer it.

choices.text: Either all earlier turns or only the customer's, chosen in code
choices.why: Right. Only the customer's turns is cheaper and loses what earlier agents found; decide it knowingly.

prompt: In the course's `minagent`, when a run stops on a limit, what does `stop()` put in the outcome's reason besides the limit itself?

choices.text: Every tool call that succeeded, by name and arguments
choices.why: Right. A stopped run hands over its results, not its plan.

choices.text: The model's plan for the steps it had not taken
choices.why: It hands over results, not a plan.

choices.text: The whole conversation, so a next run picks it up
choices.why: The conversation is not in the reason; only the calls that succeeded are listed.

choices.text: The last error message the model read
choices.why: Failed calls are left out of the handoff.

prompt: Which exceptions does `minagent`'s `Agent.call` catch and turn into an error result when a tool's function raises?

choices.text: Every exception, so that a run never crashes
choices.why: Catching everything would hide failures the model cannot fix.

choices.text: `TimeoutError`, reported as a budget stop
choices.why: Budgets are checked before each request, not caught as exceptions.

choices.text: Only `LookupError` and `ValueError`; the rest propagate and stop the run
choices.why: Right. Only expected errors are caught; anything else stops the run loudly, as lesson 4 argued.

choices.text: Errors raised by `jsonschema` during validation
choices.why: Validation collects problems with `iter_errors` and returns them; no exception is involved.

prompt: Why does `minagent`'s `record` append each step to the trace file as the run goes, instead of writing the trace once at the end?

choices.text: Because JSON has no way to hold a whole run in one object
choices.why: It could; the reason given is surviving a crash.

choices.text: So a crash leaves the steps before it on disk
choices.why: Right. One JSON line per step, written as it happens.

choices.text: So the model reads its earlier steps from the file
choices.why: The model reads the conversation, not the trace file.

choices.text: Because Ollama refuses requests bigger than one step of trace
choices.why: Ollama never sees the trace file.

prompt: In the course's run where the customer typed `M1047`, step 1 carried 434 input tokens and step 2 only 166, although step 2's request held everything step 1's did. Why?

choices.text: Ollama had cached step 1's prompt, and cached tokens go uncounted
choices.why: No. The adapter adds the cached tokens back into `tokens_in`, so they are counted.

choices.text: The loop drops earlier steps from the conversation once a call fails
choices.why: No. `Agent.run` appends to `messages` and never removes anything.

choices.text: The template leaves the tools out when a tool result comes last
choices.why: Right. Lesson 1 found it: the tool definitions are written in only when the last message is the user's.

choices.text: The schema refusal replaced the call's arguments with an error
choices.why: No. The error went back as a tool result; the call stayed in the conversation as it was.

prompt: The course warns against a loop that retries a model request on top of the SDK's own retries. With two layers of three attempts each, how many requests does one failing call become?
At the top of each step, `minagent`'s `Agent.run` checks the conditions that stop a run and then asks the model. Put these in the order the code does them.
items: Is the token budget used up?
Is the time budget used up?
Have three steps in a row had only errors?
Send the request with `model.complete`

prompt: In the course's lab, the OpenAI Agents SDK sent `get_order` with `"strict": true`. What did it change in the schema so that strict mode could work?

choices.text: It rewrote the schema with Python's `str()`, single quotes and `None` included

prompt: Where does the OpenAI Agents SDK send its traces when nothing about tracing is configured?

choices.text: To a `trace.jsonl` file in the working directory

choices.text: Nowhere; tracing stays off until you turn it on
choices.why: Tracing is on by default.

choices.text: To Ollama, together with each model request

choices.text: To OpenAI's servers

prompt: The course's `oa_guard.py` attaches an input guardrail to its refunds agent. According to the lesson, which of these is not a guardrail's job?

choices.text: Running a check that calls another model

prompt: With `failure_error_function` set, a malformed id reached the model as `ModelBehaviorError: Invalid JSON input for tool get_order`. Why does the lesson still call this vaguer than lesson 4's message?

prompt: In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a run that stopped at a call to a tool with `needs_approval=True` is continued by calling `result.___()`, recording approve or reject on what it returns, and running that again.

choices.text: People answer faster when fewer questions reach them
choices.why: Asking only where it matters is a separate habit; this one is about who enforces a limit.

choices.text: Code can confirm who the customer is, and a person cannot
choices.why: The rule is an amount limit, not an identity check.

choices.text: A person should judge, not enforce a limit
choices.why: Right. A rule with a right answer belongs in a program; the person is asked what only a person can decide.

prompt: The platform's own audit, internal/audit, does two things that role_host.py's role-audit.jsonl does not, and a production agent's audit should. Which two?

choices.text: It is append-only, and it names the person behind the agent
choices.why: Right. A correction is a new entry, and an approved refund should carry the agent and who said yes.

choices.text: It is encrypted, and it leaves out the arguments of each call
choices.why: Arguments are kept on purpose, and encryption is not what the lesson names.

choices.text: It records refusals and the run id
choices.why: role-audit.jsonl already records both.

choices.text: It is written by the server, and it keeps approved actions alone
choices.why: The host writes the record here because it sees every decision, and refusals belong in it.

prompt: Match each actor, from internal/audit and from role_host.py's audit, to what it stands for.

pairs.right: a person, named as they were at the time
the platform on its own: a scheduled job, a webhook, a retry
an agent acting for the business, named as itself

right_distractors: an entry whose actor was left out

prompt: In the cost lesson's second run of the same question, how many tokens of its first request did Ollama reuse from the run before?
cost_run.py llama3.2:3b --cache --stamp put the time of each request at the top of the system prompt. How many input tokens did that run read fresh across its two requests?
The same question's first request took 10,447 ms in one run and 3,955 ms in the next. What does the cost lesson say made the difference?

choices.text: The second run's answer was shorter
choices.why: Both first requests wrote a tool call of under 20 tokens.

choices.text: Ollama wrote output faster the second time
choices.why: Output is produced one token at a time either way.

choices.text: The second run used the smaller model
choices.why: Both runs used llama3.2:3b.

choices.text: It reused 847 tokens instead of reading 994
choices.why: Right. Reading a long prompt is the biggest part of the wait on a CPU.

prompt: From the timings of cost_run.py, the lesson draws three rules for a faster agent. Put them in order of effect, largest first.
items: Fewer steps
Shorter output where output is not the product
A smaller model where it is enough

prompt: In limits.py, the anthropic SDK retried two 529 failures by itself and the call then succeeded. Why does the lesson conclude that a tool call that changes something should be safe to repeat?

choices.text: Retries skip the rate limit, so they land sooner
choices.why: A retry counts against the rate limit like any request.

choices.text: The SDK retries a request only once it knows that repeating it is harmless
choices.why: It retried the 529s without knowing anything about what the request did.

choices.text: A retry is a new request: any work the failed attempt did gets done again
choices.why: Right. An idempotency key, or a check that the action was not already done, makes the second attempt harmless.

choices.text: A call that succeeds after retries comes back with isError
choices.why: It came back as an ordinary answer, with nothing saying it had been retried.

prompt: llama3.2:1b read the same prompt in about half the time of llama3.2:3b, and then sent a broken tool call. How does the lesson say to decide which tasks a smaller model can carry?

choices.text: By the number of input tokens each task needs
choices.why: The smaller model reads the same tokens; the question is what it can do.

choices.text: By testing it
choices.why: Right. Not by assumption; a router then sends the easy questions to it.

choices.text: By sending it every task and retrying failures on the large one
choices.why: The lesson routes with something cheap, after testing what the small model carries.

choices.text: By its price per token on the provider's page
choices.why: A price says what it costs, not what it can do.
